en: From the *Huiyuan Waizhuan*:
"The foreign sound of the Dharma has gradually reached my ears.
Master Huiyuan said daily, 'I do not know how it is that Dao’an’s lectures and praises have yielded so much understanding.'"
May I one day again ascend the high seat and bestow upon all sentient beings the fruits of the ten stages. Whether there be calamities or not,
whether there be heterodoxy or orthodoxy— [may this be so].
Those with signs and those without signs are all brought to extinction through nirvana.
In a mere instant, the lecture concluded and the men and women dispersed together.
The Master returned to his residence; once he had rested in the main hall, he ascended to his seat.
Then, with her sleeves covering her face, she went directly before the Excellency and addressed him, saying:
"It was just as you were at Shengguang Temple, listening to the Venerable Dao’an lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*."
Furthermore, he heard what Dharma was being taught: the Nirvāṇa Sūtra,
whose meaning is immeasurable and boundless.
"Lord, how much of the sutras do you remember?
Why do you remain silent and say nothing?
You have not spoken even a single verse or half-verse for the sake of your wife."
The Lord said,
"Has the Lady finished reciting the praises of the Lotus Sutra?
The Lady replied:
"I have previously read the Lotus Sutra.
Your Excellency said that according to the sutra, if one does not request it to be preached, one will certainly not listen to it."
The lady said, "I pray that you,
my lord, will briefly explain for those of high and low status within this household how much [of the Dharma] there is, so that their minds may be opened and awakened.
The lord replied:
Daode explained the meaning of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for the lady.
The lady then gave instructions to her household to sweep and sprinkle the halls and pavilions.
She prepared high seats and summoned more than three hundred members of her family, both great and small, noble and humble, to assemble together before the hall.
"Please, my lord, explain the meaning within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
All these people shall listen in silence.
That night, the lord first explained the eight sufferings to his wife.
The first discourse on the cycle of birth describes the suffering of birth.
As for the suffering of birth, it refers to the physical body;
when one is conceived, one takes refuge in the mother’s womb.
In the period leading up to the month of birth, it is like butter and curd;
within ninety days, the form is thus completed.
If it is male, he remains on the mother’s left side.
The girl was in her mother’s right flank;
clinging closely and pressed near the heart and liver, she received the vital breath and formed her shape,
thereby undergoing various sufferings.
The wise and the foolish are of one and the same rank, and the noble and the base are likewise equal;
the grace of the compassionate mother should not be of two kinds.
For a mother eating hot rice is no different from her body being boiled in a cauldron of boiling water.
When the mother eats cold things, it is as if she were in the Cold Ice Hell;
when the mother is full, it is as if she were between a pair of tongs;
when the mother is hungry, the child undergoes the suffering of being suspended upside down.
When the ten months are complete and the time for birth approaches,
the hundred joints open and expand as if being sawn apart;
one’s four limbs feel broken and the five viscera ache with pain.
No different from being wounded by a blade,
how does this differ from being sliced by a sword?
Through thousands of births and ten thousands of deaths, one immediately faints and loses consciousness, no longer knowing life.
If the hanging thread had not forgotten to revive him,
the mother and child would have been separated in an instant,
their blood like that of slaughtered sheep.
While my mother was in a state of confusion and distress, she asked whether it was a boy or a girl.
She thought that if it were a girl,
at least they could part ways safely and well.
If one is such a person of the Way,
then amidst the total forgetfulness of the hundred joints' aching pains and dizziness, they immediately break into a smile;
this is what is called a filial son.
If one were my contrary son, how could he have been born?
While still within his mother's womb, he caused her unease;
he kicked and trampled his mother without ceasing for even a moment.
Suddenly it dwells upon the heart, and suddenly it reaches the waist;
there is no place among the five viscera where it does not arrive.
When ten months are complete, it is born.
At that time, he grasped his mother’s heart and liver with his hands and trampled upon her hip bones with his feet;
for three mornings and five days, he refused to be at peace.
From this point on, my mother’s life-force suddenly turned away.
As her mother watched, she saw that she was dying; her cries shook the earth as if a sword had struck her heart.
"Brothers, you must quickly devise a plan for your mother."
An enemy or creditor will not rest until they have taken one's life;
since one must first endure for the sake of one's child, one must subsequently die—
this very process constitutes birth.
"It is you, my lord.
Furthermore, I shall explain to my lady the suffering of old age. As for what is called the suffering of old age:
though a person may live for a hundred years, it passes in an instant, like a spark of fire."
At seventy or eighty, one's physical strength and vigor decline.
What was once a voice like a bird and a countenance like spring flowers has now,
in old age, become like autumn grass.
The sinews and skin are parched like the feathers of a crane;
sight and hearing are impaired, unable to distinguish between blue and yellow;
the four limbs are heavy and weary, and the hundred bones ache with pain.
As one moves further from heaven, one should draw nearer to the earth.
Lying upon the bed at night, turning over and over a thousand times and ten thousand ways,
at that time one is unable to attend to worldly affairs, as if in a dream.
If the peach and plum trees by the roadside bloom in flower year after year,
where are those who once gazed upon them with joyful faces now?
Should old age and illness come to invade you, what then?
White hair has no way to turn black again.
The vigor of former times withers away with the eight seasons;
the rosy complexion of old days changes with the four times of the year.
All such people grow old;
whether noble or humble, they are the same.
No distinction is made between the wise and the foolish.
It is not as if one can simply endure this shared suffering of old age;
one must quickly cultivate fields of merit.
Human life passes away moment by moment, and we see it slipping away with every passing day.
One must exercise great care;
then one may practice cultivation.
Once this body is lost, there is no way to regain it again.
This is precisely what is called the suffering of old age.
That night, the noble sir explained the suffering of his illness to his wife,
and she heard it as well.
What is meant by "that which exists"?
Within the four great elements, how could there ever be any reality?
They are merely a provisional combination of various conditions: earth, water, fire, and wind.
If even a single pulse is disordered, this is illness.
When it suddenly arises and becomes heavy upon the bed,
the soul and spirit are unsettled and the five spirits are all lost.
The tongue becomes parched and the brain shrivels, causing a headache;
the hundreds of joints feel as if they are being sawn apart.
One suffers through day and night without any prospect of respite.
One seeks life but cannot find it; one seeks death but cannot find it.
The wondrous arts of this world can only treat those who still possess their allotted lifespan.
Once life has ended, how could they be saved? How could they be healed?
Medicines could not heal the damage;
for many days and nights, he endured various great sufferings.
Even if one were to apply the *kṣīra-pāyasa* (milk-rice) medicine or perform acupuncture with a *śatapattra* (peacock-feather) needle.
When the disease of death arrives, nothing can be done to avert it.

Yet worldly people, deludedly accepting false teachings, become ill before they even have the illness; they then falsely accuse gods and ghosts, burn paper money to appease them, and recklessly slaughter living beings.
Such people fall into hell; their maximum lifespan does not exceed a hundred years.

Of those hundred years, seven-tenths are lost early on, leaving only three-tenths. Even if one could enjoy a full hundred years, how much time would there actually be for a human life lived in this world?
If there were such a marvelous art,
why would those who possess a thousand-year lifespan not apply their minds to it?
One must reflect three times before recklessly accepting the deceptive claims of a master.
This is what is called the suffering of illness. Tonight, for my lady’s sake,
the four elements are about to return to extinction, and her soul and spirit are being crushed by the wind.
Brothers and elder siblings bid eternal farewell; mothers and fathers are forever separated.
Wives, children, sons, and daughters can never meet again.
Friends and associates pass by in a mere instant.
There is no way for us to see each other again.
You may take the gold, silver, and money as you please;
however, the shop, storehouse, and estates cannot be taken away.
Through the suffering of death caused by craving and attachment, the four great elements separate;
the soul and spirit fly away, and one knows not where they have gone.
When the three-inch tongue-root is severed, that is precisely the beginning of the next life.
When one person dies, when will they be reborn?
Śroṇa, regarding the discourse on the death of heroes, one obtains merit;
according to one's karma, one receives its fruit and is assigned to whatever realm it corresponds to.
Some dwell in the hells, some in the heavens, some as animals, and some as hungry ghosts;
thus they revolve through the six realms of existence without respite.
To obtain a human body once again is as rare as finding one in ten thousand.
"This is precisely what is called the suffering of death;
you, my lord, are such a person.
He then explained the suffering of the five aggregates to the lady.
Regarding the suffering of the five aggregates:
human life in this world is like the passage of day and night;
thick blood and skin, along with fine silken garments, envelop the body.
Within the five aggregates, the seven apertures constantly flow;
internally harboring the stench of excrement and filth, with wandering blood and bones, look outward at this mere bag of pus.
Mucus and saliva flow incessantly day and night, making every part unbearable.
There is absolutely no reality in what one desires;
it all arises from three inches of breath.
This is the sprout of the three poisons.
The five viscera are the root of the five desires;
thus, the Great Master had this verse:
"Thin skin envelops pus and blood, while sinews bind together stinking bones."
From head to foot,
the entire body is a flowing stream of pus;
such is what is called the mass of suffering.
The oppression of the body is what is called the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-duḥkha*).
My lord, on this very night, you further explained to my lady the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks (*apriya-saṃprayoga-duḥkha*):
in life, each person possesses their own particular things.
May those possessing merit seek unsurpassed bodhi;
furthermore, throughout the three periods of time,
may they attain the blessings of human and celestial rebirths.
How many are able to enjoy worldly glory?
Having sought wealth and resources among men,
they meet with untimely death midway along the path.
If one seeks gold, silver, and fine silks, one’s heart will be filled with glory for kalpa after kalpa;
yet even if one obtains food and clothing sufficient for oneself, it will never be enough.
Brothers and sisters must each provide for their own relief and healing.
Having given birth to sons and raised daughters, each seeks their own path;
if one did not plant seeds in previous lives nor cultivate merit over kalpas,
yet desires worldly glory, it will not be attained.
One must have cultivated merit in this present life.
This morning, I earnestly exhorted the assembly to understand that clothing and food are the fixed dwellings established by one's past lives;
as the Master has a verse on this, it is certain to be realized this year.
If one does not sow the seeds for next year's grain this year, how can there be a harvest next year?
Since existence is certain in this life,
why not cultivate the path for the next?
"To have such great merit in a future life—
this is precisely what is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
That night, the noble sir further explained to his wife the suffering of encountering those one hates.
Regarding the suffering of association with the disliked:
when people live in this world, desire dwells within their hearts;
seeing another's wife, they immediately seek to possess her.
Once one has obtained a wife and children, before even two or three years have passed, a son is born or a daughter is conceived.
To what does this serve as a metaphor? It is a premonition.
If one gathers flowers like a butterfly, circling only within the void,
suddenly one sees a single cluster of vermilion blossoms and immediately reaches out to grasp their fragrant petals.
Unaware of the spider upon it, [the cocoon] formed itself into a dense mass,
winding around it hundreds and thousands of times;
the butterfly was thus enveloped within its midst.
"Ten thousand people have no way to escape;
this is the suffering of the predestined.
The attachment of ordinary beings to form is likewise thus."
Upon seeing others who were young, they immediately conceived feelings of lustful attachment.
As the years and months passed, they eventually had sons and daughters.
Once these children grew up and reached adulthood, they became unfilial toward their parents, and their five heinous crimes filled the heavens.

One does not associate with the company of the wise; one wanders among the ignorant and speaks without understanding the need for threefold reflection. With a foolish mouth, one offends both one's six kin and one's elders.
If such a person remains within the home, they immediately waste the mental and physical energies of others.
Or if one must always be filled with anxiety and fear when venturing abroad,
this is precisely what is called "generating many enemies," which continues without end through every lifetime.
Through the skillful cause of urging the audience with words of suffering, they will understand:
if one wishes to be free from enmity in future lives,
it is better to cultivate pure conduct in this very life than to wait for the next.
Forever separated from my kinsmen, my heart swells with distress.
Among the causal conditions for men and women, there are many and few.
Regarding this, the Great Master has a verse:
Since beginningless kalpas, I have been submerged in the deep current;
I have wandered through the six realms of rebirth everywhere.
If I do not now, in this life, sever it with fierce resolve, [I shall continue in suffering].
"When enemies meet to settle their grievances, when will it ever end?
This is what is called the suffering of encountering those one hates.
That night, the noble lord further explained to his consort the suffering of being separated from those one loves.
Thus, a son was raised in the family;
his parents cherished him as if he were a precious pearl or jade.
When he grew up into an adult and could just distinguish east from west, he was already capable.
He immediately departed from his hometown and left his village;
his parents, with hearts hanging in anxiety day and night,
waited for him as they leaned against the door each morning, weeping in sorrow.
From this point on, the illness took hold in his mind;
he wondered when he would see the medicine that sustains life and sleep.
Suddenly, the winter season arrived, and all his kinsmen were before his eyes.
Suddenly remembering the man who was outside, his breath was immediately choked and his chest filled with rage;
this is what is called the suffering of separation from the beloved.
My lord, tonight’s discourse on the eight sufferings that torment one has now concluded.
All those in the residence—more than three hundred people, both young and old, noble and humble alike—prostrated themselves in thanks.
As for Sanqing, he shed tears profusely because of this auspicious occasion;
yet, Sanqing did not speak a word.
He reflected within his mind:
"I recall that in the past, when I was at Mount Tai,
I first dared to lecture on this very title of the sutra."
Great rocks shook and the hundred grasses bent their bodies;
auspicious birds and spiritual fowl flew in from all directions until they filled the air like a portentous cloud, never dispersing but constantly roaming beside the Purple Palace.
Auspicious vapors swirled and did not depart from the side of the vermilion tower.

The various devas heard the Dharma, and the ten classes of beings heard the sutra; whether possessing form or lacking form, whether with marks or markless, all attained nirvana and entered parinirvāṇa.
Having finished his reflections, Shanqing’s eyes were filled with tears.
The Lord Marquis, surprised by this, asked Shanqing,
"I have been expounding the sutras for you."
"What matter or principle causes you to weep so frequently?
For now, whom do you harbor resentment against? Speak quickly and explain the circumstances; if you do not speak, look upon this staff as it strikes you.
Shanqing stepped forward and addressed the official, saying:
"This lowly slave harbors no resentment toward others;
it is only because people say that Master An’s preaching of the Dharma is never impartial.
The young master said:
This is the Venerable Dao’an, who has come to Liangzhong himself to lecture and offer praises.
Princes, dukes, generals, and ministers listen to his preaching every day;
you have never even seen him preach the Dharma.
"How can you know that his preaching and praise were not impartial?
Shanqing stepped forward and addressed the official, saying, "Last night,
Shanqing followed my master into the temple, but being shut out at the gate, I was unable to hear the sutra."
He then realized that Master An’s preaching of the Dharma was not impartial.
Although this lowly slave dwells in an inferior station,
his understanding of the Buddha-dharma is no different from that of the purple-robed and black-robed monks.
The Dharma should be non-dual.
From this path, the teachings established by Ananda were unable to be equalized; those who do not understand the transmission of the Dharma cannot enter the three stages.
Furthermore, regarding the four modes of birth and the ten classes of beings, they are mutually public. It is said: [text follows].
What are those called the four modes of birth, the ten classes of beings, and the three grades of persons?
Explain these to me in detail so that my mind may be opened to understanding and I may clearly comprehend the Buddha-dharma.
Shanqing said:
"As for the three types of people, my disciple is the first;
the sick child is the second; and those bound and imprisoned are the third."
Third, the Dharma Master, who is not a person of independent status, does not understand the skillful means while seated upon the high throne;
his pervasive transmission reaches only the ears of those belonging to the three lower classes. Such is the fault.
For this reason, when preaching the Dharma, one does not understand equality.
The Duke asked:
"What are the four modes of birth and the ten classes of beings?"
Shanqing addresses the Excellency:
The "four modes of birth" refer to viviparous, oviparous, moisture-born, and transformational birth;
these constitute the four modes of birth.

The ten classes consist of those with form and those without form; those with characteristics and those without characteristics; those that are neither with nor without characteristics; and those with four feet, two feet, many feet, or no feet.
These are called the ten classes.
The Excellency said to Shanqing, "I do not understand; please explain it to me in detail.
Observe me as I shall abandon heterodoxy and return [to the truth]."
Zhengshanqing said, "Those born from a womb are people of the Dharma.
Two men came from the north to enter the monastery to listen to the sutras;
one was not such a person, yet he entered the monastery and listened to the sutras.
As soon as one person realized they possessed this greedy nature,
he immediately turned back and departed.
That man was able to enter the monastery.
While one person was seated in the Hall of Good Dharma listening to the wondrous Dharma for oneself, it entered their heart and body, and they immediately felt joy arise in their mind.
Suddenly, remembering those who had not come, their heart immediately became filled with forgetfulness.
Even if there were words that could be heard and accepted, one would remain in a state of persistent confusion,
like a child in the mother’s womb whose sight is obstructed by floating clouds;
in the blink of an eye, one would fall once again into the cycle of birth from a womb.
Those born from eggs are likewise people who listen to the Dharma;
therefore, they come to enter the monastery to hear the sutras and sit before the Hall of Good Dharma with hearts intent on devotion.
The Dharma Master did not understand.
He merely spoke of external conditions and explained the nature of phenomena to sentient beings who were bewildered;
it was difficult to comprehend and difficult to know.
Feeling incessant distress,
they subsequently fall among those born from eggs.
As for those born from moisture:
Such persons receive many secret teachings;
having obtained even a single phrase or a single verse, they never impart them to others, being instead consumed by greed and attachment for their own benefit,
and failing to understand how to proclaim them for the sake of the assembly.
By these causes and conditions, they fall among those born from moisture.
As for those born by transformation:
having entered a temple in the north to listen to the Dharma, they obtain a single phrase of the sublime Dharma.
Through discernment, one attains the immeasurable and boundless.
By expounding the meaning and the text, one draws others toward transformation and edification.
It is like a single lamp on the Ganges River being lit, which then illuminates ten lamps, then a hundred, then a thousand, and even hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of lamps.
That the lamp is passed from lamp to lamp without interruption is precisely what is called "birth by transformation.
Thereupon, the Marquis asked,
"What are the ten categories?"
Shanqing said: "First, regarding those with form:
upon seeing a clay grotto or a sculpted image, one immediately bows with a sincere heart and says directly, 'The Buddha is like Mount Sumeru.
To see the form and give rise to the mind [of faith] is what is meant by 'having form.'"
The second is that which is formless:
it does not establish a locus for nature, nor is nature perceived therein;
it is like the moon in water or the wind in space.
All phenomena are non-existent and nothing at all;
this is precisely what is called "formlessness.
Third is that which possesses characteristics.
While walking through the streets, he saw a person of upright appearance and said,
"This object from the past has been cultivated and has now entered the temple.
Upon hearing the Dharma, he saw that the Dharma Master was stout and fair-skinned.
Thereupon, a mind of attachment arose within him.
He was immediately bound by it;
and once there was this binding, [he remained].
There is, then, conceptual construction;
since there is conceptual construction, there is ignorance;
since there is ignorance, there is affliction.
Since afflictions exist, there is cyclic existence; since cyclic existence exists,
there are the physical and mental continuities of hell that one undergoes for many kalpas as a result of transgressions,
experiencing their suffering without fail.
This is what is called "having characteristics.
As for the fourth, "no-characteristics":
all phenomena are empty.
How could there ever have been reality?
There are no traces to the east or west,
and no footprints to the south or north.
This matter does not reside within body or mind;
it transcends the three realms as a single unity.
This is precisely what is called "formlessness" (animitta).
Fifth, regarding the characteristic of non-existence:
it should be stated that what exists immediately becomes non-existent upon being spoken of;
it should be established that what exists does not persist and immediately returns to non-existence; this should be believed.
That which exists through non-belief immediately returns to the non-existence of the ten thousand dharmas;
it does not reside in the mind or body.
This is precisely what is called the characteristic of non-existence.
The sixth is not the signless:
it is without speech, without words, without going, without coming, without movement, and without thought;
non-arising and non-ceasing is itself suchness (tathatā).
The absence of going and the absence of coming is precisely the Buddha-nature;
this is what is called "not being without characteristics.
Seventh, regarding those with two feet:
In this human life, there is the body and consciousness;
these two, together with the fleeting name, constitute the "two-legged" being.
Yet, in an instant, one may possess a body while lacking consciousness.
Suddenly there is wisdom, yet no body.
It is precisely when this body and wisdom do not meet that one does not encounter delusion;
if body and wisdom were to meet, one would sink into the evil realms.
He was then born into the realm of the Buddha-way.
There is a verse by the Great Master:
"When the body is born, wisdom is not yet born; when wisdom is born,"
The body has already grown old; the body regrets that wisdom arose too late.
Wisdom regrets that the body was born too early; body and wisdom did not meet.
How many times have we experienced this aging of the body and this wisdom?
If one encounters [this] immediately, one attains the Way of Buddhahood.
Possessing this body and wisdom is what is called "the two feet.
As for the eighth, the "four feet":
The four great elements of human life belong to earth, water, fire, and wind.
The four directions and the four oceans are what are called the "four legs.
As for the "many-legged" ninth [element]:

He penetrates all phenomena such that there is nothing he does not understand; regarding worldly affairs, he comprehends them all entirely. When questioned on any of the various scriptures, there is no answer he cannot provide.
The twelve divisions of the honored sutras are recorded within his mind.
This is what is called "many-footed.
Tenth, as for the "footless":
although they are human beings, they are incapable of managing affairs and lack eloquence.
Their behavior is no different from that of animals;
this is precisely what is meant by "footless.
Thus far, these ten categories are each distinct from one another.
If you have further doubts,
feel free to ask whatever you wish;
upon hearing these words, the Excellency felt as if nectar had entered his heart.
When the lady opened it, it was as if nectar had been poured over her head.
She called for Shanqing, saying, "Come closer; just now..."
"According to what you have proclaimed,
it would be better for Dao'an and me to discuss this further,
so that my mind may be opened to understanding and I may clearly grasp the Buddha-dharma."
Thereupon, Shanqing explained the twelve links of dependent origination for the Chancellor:

ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

With the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness, there is the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form, there is the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases, there is the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling, there is the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving, there is the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging, there is the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence, there is the cessation of birth; and with the cessation of birth, there is the cessation of old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
When Master Xiang heard of these twelve links of dependent origination, he repeatedly exclaimed, "Excellent!
At that time, the lady sighed with admiration, realizing she had gained immeasurable fields of merit.
Upon this auspicious occasion, she descended from her high seat and addressed Master Xiang.
It is just as with Dharma Master Dao’an:
it would be like attempting to construct a hall or palace in the midst of empty space;
one could never bring it to completion, and even as it was about to be finished, it would inevitably collapse.
"Though this lowly slave’s body is of inferior station, the Buddha-dharma is uniform;
our robes differ, but our essence is not of two kinds.
This slave now wishes to accompany you, my lord, into the monastery to meet with the Dharma Master Dao’an at the same time."
Therefore, Master Yixiang said:
"If you have the intention,
I shall not obstruct you."
Thereupon, the Lord and Lady ordered Shanqing to bathe in scented water within the western courtyard, change his clothes, and be released.
He was told to return to his room to rest until the following day.
At dawn, there was another instruction.
Once Shanqing had returned to his room,
he settled his mind and purified his intentions until daybreak.
He did not sleep any further.
At the moment he was about to enter the court,
Shanqing also followed the Excellency into the inner palace.
The Excellency retired from court and returned to his residence to rest.
He then summoned Shanqing and said,
"This Daoan is a preeminent monk within the realm."
"You must consider this very carefully.
Shanqing addressed the Marquis, saying,
"The worldly scholar said:"
There is a saying:
"One who enters the mountains without avoiding wolves and tigers possesses the courage of a woodcutter;
one who enters the waters without avoiding crocodiles and dragons possesses the courage of a fisherman."
But if this humble servant were to prevail in the debate against Dao’an,
it would be like a thirsty man finding water or a cold man finding fire;
I beg you, Excellency, to rest with your pillow high and be free from anxiety.
"I shall go as soon as you have finished speaking. In a mere moment, he had already arrived.
The Excellency had previously sent two hundred strings of cash.
Thereafter, Shanqing was brought into the monastery;
at that time, the assembly gathered like clouds,
and the offerings poured in like the tolling of bells.
As soon as the movement began, the lecturer and the assistant lecturer raised their voices, and the *vinaya-dhara* intoned the *brahma-svara*.
The fourfold assembly gazed upon them as if they had ascended Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa;
Dao’an wished to compare this joyful heart to that of the assembly at the Añjana Grove.
Thereupon, Dao’an personally held the *cintāmaṇi* (wish-fulfilling gem) and sat upon a precious dais;
he burned priceless precious incense and proclaimed the sublime meaning.
He raised his voice and proclaimed, reciting the title of the scripture:
"The Great Nirvana Sutra, Chapter One: The Lifespan of the Tathāgata."
Having completed the opening of the scripture, he praised the Buddha’s majestic deportment;
first manifesting the sagely excellence, he subsequently extolled the imperial virtue.

It is his humble wish that the present Emperor’s Way corresponds to that of the dragon-horses and his virtue illuminates the Golden Garden; grasping the golden mirror, he shines like the sun upon the nine heavens, and following divine light, he presides over the eight directions.

May the princes and crown princes of all kings have their golden branches forever firm and their jade leaves eternally flourishing; may the princesses possess noble dignity, purity, and virtue, shining perpetually within the court.
